# Answer

**Short answer.** The man in the white shirt is Macbeth, making his last stand on the rampart (the "bridge") of his castle, and the man who comes at him along the bridge from the right is an enemy soldier attacking him. Macbeth flings the powder into the attacker's face as a weapon: it blinds and stuns the soldier at the instant he reaches Macbeth, so that Macbeth can seize him, force him down on the parapet and hurl him off the bridge to his death. In other words the powder is thrown in self-defence, to disable an armed man who is charging him, so that he can kill him and hold the wall. In this particular production the powder is staged as a voodoo-style hex, Macbeth's sorcerer's weapon, which fits the character's belief that he is protected by the witches' charm and cannot be killed by any man "of woman born"; he laughs in triumph when the throw works.

## What the footage is

The video is the 1937 WPA film "We Work Again" (title card at the start, "Produced by the Work Projects Administration"). Its last segment (roughly 11:05 to 14:30) is the famous surviving footage of the Federal Theatre Project's all-Black "Voodoo Macbeth" (Orson Welles's staging of Shakespeare's Macbeth relocated to 19th-century Haiti, with the witches turned into voodoo priests). A theatre audience is visible in the wide shots, so everything in the scene is a staged play. The set is a jungle-castle with a raised stone rampart (the bridge) reached by a staircase at the right, an arched passage below it, and a bench on the stage floor. Published descriptions of this clip confirm it is the play's final minutes: the attacking army, Macbeth's death at the hands of Macduff, and Macbeth's severed head displayed. The bearded man in the white shirt is Macbeth (Maurice Ellis); the officer in the braided white military tunic is Macduff (Charles Collins); the figure with the towering plumed headdress standing in the alcove at the far left is the male Hecate / witch-doctor figure.

## The sequence of events I observed (timestamps are minutes:seconds into the video)

1. **11:05–11:30.** Iris-in on the stage. A group is gathered around a shrouded body laid on the bench (Lady Macbeth's corpse). The mourners leave and Macbeth, in the white shirt, is left alone beside the body, pacing and gesturing as he delivers a speech (11:30–12:12).
2. **12:12–12:20.** Macbeth, carrying a sword, runs to the staircase at the right, climbs onto the rampart and walks to its centre, then its left end. He now holds the high ground.
3. **12:25–12:28.** An officer in a light braided uniform (Macduff) enters below through the arch. Macbeth points his sword down at him and moves to the far left end of the bridge. A close-up (12:29–12:42) shows the officer, in an ornate general's tunic with a high collar, shouting angrily up at Macbeth.
4. **12:42–12:45.** A second man, in a striped shirt, climbs the staircase at the right onto the bridge and creeps toward Macbeth in a low, crouching attack posture with one arm raised.
5. **12:45.5–12:46.** The film cuts to a close-up of Macbeth at the left end of the bridge. He leans out to his right toward the oncoming man with his right arm extended, then draws his hands together, and a dense white cloud of powder bursts out of his hands and billows to the right, exactly where the attacker arrives. There is no flash frame, so this is thrown powder rather than a gunshot.
6. **12:46–12:48.5.** Inside the cloud the striped-shirt attacker appears doubled over, hands to his face, blinded and helpless. Macbeth grabs him by the shoulders, bends him over the parapet, raises his arm and strikes down at him, and then shoves the limp body over the edge. A wide shot shows the body tumbling off the bridge (12:48.5), and from then on a corpse lies on the stage floor at the lower left.
7. **12:50–12:52.** Close-up: Macbeth sits astride the parapet, legs apart, laughing broadly, an object in each hand. This is the gloating of a man who believes no ordinary soldier can touch him.
8. **12:52–13:20.** Standing at the far left of the bridge, Macbeth looks down on the officer below, who shouts and gestures up at him for almost half a minute: the two enemies are exchanging defiance before their fight.
9. **13:20.8.** The officer raises his arm straight up toward Macbeth holding a thin object, and a puff of white smoke erupts from its tip at parapet level and rises between the two men. Frame by frame the smoke starts at the top of the officer's upraised weapon, not in Macbeth's hands (Macbeth's sword hand is hanging at his other side), so this second cloud is the officer firing a pistol up at Macbeth, not a second throw by Macbeth. Macbeth ducks but is untouched, exactly as a man who believes he bears a charmed life would be; the officer flings up both arms, then runs up the staircase (13:22–13:25) and advances along the bridge from the right toward Macbeth with his sword drawn to finish the fight hand to hand.
10. **13:28–14:10.** The two duel with swords on the bridge. The cloud visible in the wide shots here is the same smoke from 13:20.8 still hanging in the air (the medium shots immediately before the cut show no fresh throw). The attacking army floods the stage below carrying branches ("Birnam Wood"), the witches with flower headdresses watch from the right end of the bridge, and Macduff overpowers Macbeth and kills him.
11. **14:10–14:30.** Macduff holds up Macbeth's severed head and the crowd hails the new king; the three witches leer over the head; the Hecate figure closes the play; "THE END".

So the moment the question describes, the man in white at the far left of the bridge throwing powder at a man running at him from the right, is the fight at 12:45–12:48 with the striped-shirt soldier.

## How I know why he throws the powder

- **The target is an attacker, not a bystander.** The striped-shirt man comes up the enemy's staircase and stalks along the bridge toward Macbeth in a crouched, arm-raised posture; Macbeth has just been threatening the officer below with his sword and has taken up a defensive position at the far end of the wall. The whole scene is the final assault on Macbeth's castle, and the men coming at him are his enemies.
- **The powder is aimed and timed like a weapon.** It leaves Macbeth's own hands as he lunges toward the oncoming man, and the cloud envelops the attacker at the moment he arrives; it is not scattered ritually into the air but thrown point-blank at a person.
- **Its effect is to disable the attacker.** The next frames show the man inside the cloud bent double with his hands over his face, unable to fight, while Macbeth calmly takes hold of him.
- **Macbeth immediately exploits that helplessness to kill him.** He pins the man on the parapet, strikes him and pushes him off the bridge; a body then lies below for the rest of the scene. So the purpose of the powder was to make the kill possible and to keep the wall.
- **Macbeth's reaction shows the intent.** Right afterward he sits on the parapet and laughs in triumph, the reaction of a man who has just dispatched an attacker exactly as he meant to.
- **The production context explains the choice of a powder rather than a plain sword blow.** This is the voodoo-themed Macbeth: the witch-doctor Hecate figure stands watching at the far left throughout, and the play's Macbeth believes the witches' charm makes him invulnerable to any man born of woman (his laughter after the kill echoes his line that he "laughs to scorn" weapons brandished by such men). Hurling a hex-powder at an attacker is that charmed confidence made visible. The next attacker, Macduff, who in the play is the one man the charm does not cover, gets past him and kills him.

The video has no audio track, so I could not hear the dialogue; the character identities and the "charm" reading come from the visible staging plus published descriptions of this well-documented clip. The observable facts, that the man in white throws the powder at an armed man charging him, that it blinds the man, and that he then throws the man off the bridge, are directly visible in the frames and do not depend on that outside knowledge.

# Analysis of the Bridge Scene in *We Work Again* (1937)

In the theatrical scene featured in the 1937 WPA documentary *We Work Again* (around the 14:07–14:09 mark), the man in the white shirt on the far left (representing Macbeth, played by Jack Carter) throws powder at the man running toward him from the right (representing Macduff, played by Maurice Ellis) during their climactic duel on the elevated stage bridge.

## Why the Man in the White Shirt Throws the Powder

1. **Voodoo Magic/Supernatural Spell Defense:** In Orson Welles' legendary 1936 stage adaptation of *Macbeth* (commonly known as the **"Voodoo Macbeth"**), the setting was transposed from medieval Scotland to 19th-century Haiti. The original three witches and Hecate were replaced by Voodoo priestesses and a male Voodoo priest (Hecate, played by Eric Burroughs). Macbeth's rise to power, sense of security, and supposed invulnerability are entirely tied to voodoo magic, charms, and prophecies. When cornered on the bridge, Macbeth throws the **voodoo ritual powder** as a desperate, supernatural spell or charm to weaken, curse, or ward off his challenger.
2. **Tactical Blinding/Disorientation:** From a practical stage-combat and narrative perspective, throwing the powder creates a sudden cloud of dust in the air. This serves as a desperate tactical move to blind, disorient, or slow down Macduff as he charges across the narrow bridge, giving Macbeth a final, defensive opportunity to strike or escape.

## How We Know This

We can confirm this through both direct visual evidence in the video and historical documentation of the production:

*   **Visual Evidence in the Video (Timestamp ~14:07 to 14:09):** 
    *   **Positioning on the Bridge:** The scene takes place on a high, vertical stage footbridge structure linking the two sides of the multi-level set.
    *   **The Characters:** On the far left of the bridge stands a man in a white period shirt (Macbeth). On the far right is another man (Macduff) preparing to charge.
    *   **The Throwing Action:** At approximately 14:07, the man in the white shirt on the far left makes a distinct throwing motion with his right hand. Immediately, a bright white cloud of powder appears near him and travels horizontally across the bridge, expanding in area (from ~800 pixels to over 1200 pixels in high-contrast analysis) as it disperses in mid-air towards the right.
    *   **The Follow-up Charge:** Immediately after the powder is thrown and begins to disperse (around 14:08), the man on the right charges through the cloud, and the two clash in hand-to-hand combat (machete/sword duel) in the middle of the bridge, confirming that the throw was a defensive mechanism initiated just before the physical confrontation.
*   **Historical and Production Context:**
    *   This footage is the only surviving record of Orson Welles's *Voodoo Macbeth*, preserved inside the 1937 WPA film *We Work Again*. 
    *   Historical analyses of the play record that Welles heavily incorporated authentic Haitian Vodou and Myalism elements, which were researched from Joseph J. Williams's 1932 book *Voodoos and Obeahs*. The use of ritual powders (resembling cornmeal, flour, or "goofer dust" used in Vodou to draw *veve* symbols and cast spells of invulnerability or harm) was a core aesthetic and plot device throughout the production.
    *   The throwing of powder mirrors the voodoo rituals performed by the witches and Hecate earlier in the play, where they threw flash powders and spell ingredients into cauldrons to invoke spirits and bind charms. Macbeth, having put his ultimate faith in these voodoo spirits, mimics their practices in his final moments of desperation.
